cardDefinitions.noteEn: Metido is the completed-action form of meter. With a person and a situation introduced by en, it can describe getting or drawing that person into the situation.

example.es: Han metido a Leo en un problema.
example.en: They have gotten Leo into a problem.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: how; marks the degree of a description in lo ... que
no separate English word; completes the lo ... que degree pattern

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Lista can mean “ready” in other contexts. When it describes a person as an ability, it means “smart” or “clever.”

cardDefinitions.answerEn: rationalizing; finding plausible reasons after the fact
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Racionalizando is the -ando form of racionalizar. Here it names the activity at which the people are described as skilled.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: the (as part of cuanto más, “the more”)

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Donde has no written accent here because it links back to the available ideas and arguments rather than asking a direct or indirect question.

example.en: There are several options to choose from.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: in; required after confiar before what is trusted
on earth; the hell (informal question emphasis)
no separate English word; adds emphasis in tan solo (“only; just”)

cardDefinitions.noteEn: With el, la, lo, los, or las, mejor usually means “best.” Without one of those words, it often means “better.”
Ejem represents the sound of clearing one's throat, often to attract attention or pointedly interrupt.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say that someone gets or draws another person into a situation?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use meter a alguien en algo, changing meter for the person and time.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Meter literally means “to put.” A introduces the person affected, and en introduces the situation. With a problem, conflict, or activity, the whole pattern can mean to get or drag someone into it.

example.es: No metas a Leo en el problema.
example.en: Don't drag Leo into the problem.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you express how strikingly good, difficult, large, or similar something is?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use lo, then the describing word, then que and a verb.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Each plus sign means “followed by.” Lo stays unchanged, while the adjective—the word that describes a person or thing—matches what it describes: lo bueno for masculine and lo buena for feminine. Que introduces the clause that identifies the person or thing.

example.es: No imaginas lo difícil que es.
example.en: You can't imagine how difficult it is.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say that something is so strongly one way that a result follows?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use tan before the describing word, then que before the result.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Each plus sign means “followed by.” Tan gives the degree, the adjective describes the person or thing, and que introduces what follows because of that degree.

example.es: La caja es tan pesada que no puedo moverla.
example.en: The box is so heavy that I can't move it.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say that the more one thing happens, the less another thing happens?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Start the first part with cuanto más and the second part with menos.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Cuanto has no accent in this comparison because it is not asking “how much.” The verbs and descriptions after más and menos change normally for the people, things, and times involved.

example.es: Cuanto más duermo, menos cansado estoy.
example.en: The more I sleep, the less tired I am.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say that you clearly understand or feel sure about something?
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Tener literally means “to have,” but this pattern says that an idea is clear in someone's mind. Claro can match a named feminine or plural thing: tengo clara la fecha and tengo claras las reglas.

example.es: Tengo clara la fecha de la reunión.
example.en: I'm clear about the meeting date.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: What word follows confiar before the person, thing, or action that is trusted?
cardDefinitions.noteEn: The plus sign means “followed by.” En can introduce a person or thing, or an action verb in its unchanged dictionary form. That unchanged form is called the infinitive and ends in -ar, -er, or -ir.

example.en: I trust that I can finish today.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How can you add exasperation or disbelief to a question?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Put demonios after qué, dónde, cómo, or another question word.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: The plus sign means “followed by.” Demonios is not literal here; it adds an informal force similar to “on earth” or, more strongly, “the hell.”

example.en: Where on earth are my keys?

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How can you say “only” or “just” with a little extra emphasis?
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Tan solo works as one fixed expression here. Tan does not keep its usual separate meaning “so”; the pair is similar to solamente or solo.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say that someone does something as well as they can?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use lo mejor que followed by a form of poder that matches the person and time.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: The plus sign means “followed by.” Lo and mejor stay fixed. Poder changes: puedo for “I can,” puedes for “you can,” and podemos for “we can.”

example.en: We cook as well as we can.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: What does sala de profesores refer to at a school?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: It is the teachers' lounge or staff room.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Sala names a room, de links it to its users, and profesores means teachers here. English naming varies by region between “teachers' lounge” and “staff room.”

example.es: Nos reunimos en la sala de profesores.
example.en: We meet in the staff room.

regions.labelEs: MIS ESTUDIANTES ME HAN METIDO EN OTRA DISCUSIÓN POLÍTICA.

applications.explanationEn: Han changes for the plural students, while metido is the completed-action form of meter.
Me identifies the person drawn in, metido supplies meter in the completed-action form, and en introduces the situation.
A veces marks the event as something that happens on some occasions.

regions.labelEs: ÚLTIMAMENTE ME MOLESTAN LOS DEBATES POLÍTICOS. SÓLO MUESTRAN LO BUENA QUE ES LA GENTE LISTA RACIONALIZANDO.

applications.explanationEn: Lo marks degree, buena gives the feminine description of gente, and que es introduces who has that quality.

regions.labelEs: EL MUNDO ES TAN COMPLICADO QUE CUANTO MÁS APRENDO, MENOS CLARO LO TENGO TODO. HAY DEMASIADAS IDEAS Y ARGUMENTOS DONDE ESCOGER. ¿CÓMO PUEDO CONFIAR EN SABER LA VERDAD SOBRE ALGUNA COSA?

applications.explanationEn: Tan gives the degree of complicado, and que introduces what follows from that degree.
Cuanto más introduces the increasing learning, while menos introduces the decreasing clarity.
Claro is placed first for emphasis, while lo and todo identify what the speaker does not have clearly understood.
Cómo carries an accent because it directly asks how.
Confiar requires en before the trusted action, and saber remains in its unchanged dictionary form.

regions.labelEs: Y SI TODO LO QUE SÉ ES TAN ENDEBLE, ¿QUÉ DEMONIOS HAGO ENSEÑANDO?

applications.explanationEn: Lo que refers neutrally to the whole body of knowledge rather than to a named masculine or feminine noun.
Qué carries an accent because it directly asks what.
Demonios adds exasperated emphasis to the question word qué rather than referring literally to demons.
Enseñando is the -ando form that names the teaching activity occurring while the speaker questions his role.

regions.labelEs: SUPONGO QUE TAN SOLO LO HACES LO MEJOR QUE PUEDES. NADIE PUEDE IMPARTIR VERDADES UNIVERSALES PERFECTAS A SUS ALUMNOS.

applications.explanationEn: Tan solo functions together as the fixed expression “only” here.
Lo mejor que stays fixed, and puedes is the form of poder that matches the person being addressed.
